claim: Mutations in CHD7 are the major cause of CHARGE syndrome
source: Mutations in CHD7 are the major cause of CHARGE syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder with an estimated prevalence of 1/15,000.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the citation context of the manuscript

claim: CHARGE syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder
source: Mutations in CHD7 are the major cause of CHARGE syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder with an estimated prevalence of 1/15,000.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the inheritance pattern of CHARGE syndrome

claim: CHARGE syndrome has an estimated prevalence of 1/15,000
source: Mutations in CHD7 are the major cause of CHARGE syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder with an estimated prevalence of 1/15,000.
evidence: This is a cited epidemiological statistic

claim: Chd7 haploinsufficiency results in reduced Fgf8 expression in the isthmus organiser
source: Using mouse models, we show that Chd7 haploinsufficiency results in reduced Fgf8 expression in the isthmus organiser (IsO), an embryonic signalling centre that directs early cerebellar development.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: The isthmus organiser is an embryonic signalling centre that directs early cerebellar development
source: Using mouse models, we show that Chd7 haploinsufficiency results in reduced Fgf8 expression in the isthmus organiser (IsO), an embryonic signalling centre that directs early cerebellar development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the IsO

claim: Chd7 and Fgf8 loss-of-function alleles interact during cerebellar development
source: Consistent with this observation, Chd7 and Fgf8 loss-of-function alleles interact during cerebellar development.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing synergistic effects in double mutants

claim: CHD7 associates with Otx2 and Gbx2 regulatory elements
source: CHD7 associates with Otx2 and Gbx2 regulatory elements and altered expression of these homeobox genes implicates CHD7 in the maintenance of cerebellar identity during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4

claim: Altered expression of Otx2 and Gbx2 implicates CHD7 in the maintenance of cerebellar identity during embryogenesis
source: CHD7 associates with Otx2 and Gbx2 regulatory elements and altered expression of these homeobox genes implicates CHD7 in the maintenance of cerebellar identity during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of altered gene expression in mutants

claim: 35% of CHARGE syndrome patients with a proven CHD7 mutation exhibit cerebellar vermis hypoplasia
source: Finally, we report cerebellar vermis hypoplasia in 35% of CHARGE syndrome patients with a proven CHD7 mutation.
evidence: This is based on clinical data from 20 patients analyzed in the study

claim: The cerebellum is derived from dorsal rhombomere 1
source: The cerebellum is derived from dorsal rhombomere 1 (r1), the anterior-most segment of the embryonic hindbrain.
evidence: This is established developmental biology knowledge

claim: Rhombomere 1 is the anterior-most segment of the embryonic hindbrain
source: The cerebellum is derived from dorsal rhombomere 1 (r1), the anterior-most segment of the embryonic hindbrain.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge

claim: The survival and patterning of r1 is controlled by Fibroblast Growth Factor 8 (FGF8)
source: The survival and patterning of r1 is controlled by Fibroblast Growth Factor 8 (FGF8), secreted from the isthmus organiser (IsO), an organising centre located at the boundary between the embryonic midbrain (mesencephalon, mes) and r1 (reviewed by Nakamura et al., 2005; Martinez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles

claim: FGF8 is secreted from the isthmus organiser
source: The survival and patterning of r1 is controlled by Fibroblast Growth Factor 8 (FGF8), secreted from the isthmus organiser (IsO), an organising centre located at the boundary between the embryonic midbrain (mesencephalon, mes) and r1 (reviewed by Nakamura et al., 2005; Martinez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: The isthmus organiser is located at the boundary between the embryonic midbrain and r1
source: The survival and patterning of r1 is controlled by Fibroblast Growth Factor 8 (FGF8), secreted from the isthmus organiser (IsO), an organising centre located at the boundary between the embryonic midbrain (mesencephalon, mes) and r1 (reviewed by Nakamura et al., 2005; Martinez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations

claim: The IsO forms at the expression boundary of Otx2 and Gbx2
source: The IsO forms at the expression boundary of two homeobox genes: Otx2 (Orthodenticle Homeobox 2) in the anterior neural tube and, Gbx2 (Gastrulation Brain Homeobox 2), in the posterior neural tube.
evidence: This is established developmental biology knowledge

claim: Otx2 is expressed in the anterior neural tube
source: The IsO forms at the expression boundary of two homeobox genes: Otx2 (Orthodenticle Homeobox 2) in the anterior neural tube and, Gbx2 (Gastrulation Brain Homeobox 2), in the posterior neural tube.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Otx2 expression pattern

claim: Gbx2 is expressed in the posterior neural tube
source: The IsO forms at the expression boundary of two homeobox genes: Otx2 (Orthodenticle Homeobox 2) in the anterior neural tube and, Gbx2 (Gastrulation Brain Homeobox 2), in the posterior neural tube.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Gbx2 expression pattern

claim: Fgf8 expression in the IsO is initiated at early (3–5) somite stages in the mouse embryo
source: Fgf8 expression in the IsO is initiated at early (3–5) somite stages in the mouse embryo, resulting in a stable gene-regulatory network at the IsO, where (1) cross-repressive interactions between Otx2 and Gbx2 maintain the IsO, (2) Otx2 represses Fgf8 expression, thus restricting it to r1, and (3) Fgf8 and Gbx2 contribute to the maintenance of each other's expression (reviewed by Joyner et al., 2000; Martinez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Cross-repressive interactions between Otx2 and Gbx2 maintain the IsO
source: Fgf8 expression in the IsO is initiated at early (3–5) somite stages in the mouse embryo, resulting in a stable gene-regulatory network at the IsO, where (1) cross-repressive interactions between Otx2 and Gbx2 maintain the IsO, (2) Otx2 represses Fgf8 expression, thus restricting it to r1, and (3) Fgf8 and Gbx2 contribute to the maintenance of each other's expression (reviewed by Joyner et al., 2000; Martinez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Otx2 represses Fgf8 expression, thus restricting it to r1
source: Fgf8 expression in the IsO is initiated at early (3–5) somite stages in the mouse embryo, resulting in a stable gene-regulatory network at the IsO, where (1) cross-repressive interactions between Otx2 and Gbx2 maintain the IsO, (2) Otx2 represses Fgf8 expression, thus restricting it to r1, and (3) Fgf8 and Gbx2 contribute to the maintenance of each other's expression (reviewed by Joyner et al., 2000; Martinez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Fgf8 and Gbx2 contribute to the maintenance of each other's expression
source: Fgf8 expression in the IsO is initiated at early (3–5) somite stages in the mouse embryo, resulting in a stable gene-regulatory network at the IsO, where (1) cross-repressive interactions between Otx2 and Gbx2 maintain the IsO, (2) Otx2 represses Fgf8 expression, thus restricting it to r1, and (3) Fgf8 and Gbx2 contribute to the maintenance of each other's expression (reviewed by Joyner et al., 2000; Martinez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: The level of FGF gene expression and signalling from the IsO has to be tightly controlled to ensure normal cerebellar development
source: Studies in the mouse embryo have shown that the level of FGF gene expression and signalling from the IsO has to be tightly controlled to ensure normal cerebellar development.
evidence: This is established knowledge from mouse studies

claim: Altered FGF signalling in the mes/r1 region preferentially affects the development of the medial cerebellum, the vermis
source: Altered FGF signalling in the mes/r1 region preferentially affects the development of the medial cerebellum, the vermis (Xu et al., 2000; Trokovic et al., 2003; Basson et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2011), which is derived from precursors in the most anterior part of r1, closest to the source of FGF8 expression (Sgaier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: The cerebellar vermis is derived from precursors in the most anterior part of r1, closest to the source of FGF8 expression
source: Altered FGF signalling in the mes/r1 region preferentially affects the development of the medial cerebellum, the vermis (Xu et al., 2000; Trokovic et al., 2003; Basson et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2011), which is derived from precursors in the most anterior part of r1, closest to the source of FGF8 expression (Sgaier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sgaier et al., 2005

claim: Reduced FGF signalling results in hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis in mice
source: The observation that reduced FGF signalling results in hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis in mice raises the possibility that reduced FGF signalling might underlie vermis hypoplasia in certain human conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge from mouse studies

claim: FGF signalling has many essential roles during development
source: However, studies in mice have also found that FGF signalling has many essential roles during development and even small reductions in Fgf8 expression during embryonic development are incompatible with postnatal survival (Meyers et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meyers et al., 1998

claim: Even small reductions in Fgf8 expression during embryonic development are incompatible with postnatal survival
source: However, studies in mice have also found that FGF signalling has many essential roles during development and even small reductions in Fgf8 expression during embryonic development are incompatible with postnatal survival (Meyers et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meyers et al., 1998

claim: Mutations causing sufficiently reduced Fgf8 expression throughout the whole embryo to result in cerebellar defects are unlikely to yield viable offspring
source: These findings suggest that mutations causing sufficiently reduced Fgf8 expression or signalling throughout the whole embryo to result in cerebellar defects are unlikely to yield viable offspring.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that small reductions in Fgf8 are lethal

claim: A disruption of the mechanisms that regulate local Fgf8 expression at the IsO is more likely to be responsible for cerebellar vermis hypoplasia in humans than global Fgf8 reduction
source: Rather, it seems more likely that a disruption of the mechanisms that regulate local Fgf8 expression at the IsO will be responsible for cerebellar vermis hypoplasia in humans.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the lethality of global Fgf8 reduction

claim: Central nervous system defects have been reported in CHARGE syndrome
source: Central nervous system defects have been reported in CHARGE (Coloboma of the eye, Heart defects, Atresia of the choanae, Retarded growth and development, Genital anomalies and Ear malformations or deafness) syndrome (Lin et al., 1990; Tellier et al., 1998; Becker et al., 2001; Issekutz et al., 2005; Sanlaville et al., 2006; Sanlaville and Verloes, 2007; Bergman et al., 2011), including reports of cerebellar defects in pre-term CHARGE fetuses (Becker et al., 2001; Sanlaville et al., 2006; Legendre et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations

claim: Cerebellar defects have been reported in pre-term CHARGE fetuses
source: Central nervous system defects have been reported in CHARGE (Coloboma of the eye, Heart defects, Atresia of the choanae, Retarded growth and development, Genital anomalies and Ear malformations or deafness) syndrome (Lin et al., 1990; Tellier et al., 1998; Becker et al., 2001; Issekutz et al., 2005; Sanlaville et al., 2006; Sanlaville and Verloes, 2007; Bergman et al., 2011), including reports of cerebellar defects in pre-term CHARGE fetuses (Becker et al., 2001; Sanlaville et al., 2006; Legendre et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Becker et al., 2001; Sanlaville et al., 2006; Legendre et al., 2012

claim: 60–90% of individuals suspected for CHARGE syndrome have de novo, heterozygous mutations in the CHD7 gene
source: Depending on the clinical selection, 60–90% of the individuals suspected for CHARGE syndrome have de novo, heterozygous mutations in the CHD7 (Chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 7, MIM#608892) gene (Vissers et al., 2004; Bilan et al., 2012; Janssen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies

claim: CHD7 is a member of the SNF2H-like chromatin-remodelling family
source: CHD7 is a member of the SNF2H-like chromatin-remodelling family and has been shown to function as a 'transcriptional rheostat' by maintaining appropriate levels of developmental gene expression (Schnetz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CHD7 protein family

claim: CHD7 functions as a 'transcriptional rheostat' by maintaining appropriate levels of developmental gene expression
source: CHD7 is a member of the SNF2H-like chromatin-remodelling family and has been shown to function as a 'transcriptional rheostat' by maintaining appropriate levels of developmental gene expression (Schnetz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schnetz et al., 2010

claim: CHARGE syndrome shows significant clinical overlap with 22q11.2 deletion and Kallmann syndromes
source: For example, CHARGE syndrome shows significant clinical overlap with 22q11.2 deletion and Kallmann syndromes, both of which have been linked to reduced FGF signalling (Scambler, 2010; Miraoui et al., 2013; Corsten-Janssen et al., 2013; Randall et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations

claim: 22q11.2 deletion and Kallmann syndromes have been linked to reduced FGF signalling
source: For example, CHARGE syndrome shows significant clinical overlap with 22q11.2 deletion and Kallmann syndromes, both of which have been linked to reduced FGF signalling (Scambler, 2010; Miraoui et al., 2013; Corsten-Janssen et al., 2013; Randall et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations

claim: Mice heterozygous for the Chd7XK403 gene-trap allele phenocopy several aspects of CHARGE syndrome
source: We previously reported that mice heterozygous for the Chd7XK403 gene-trap allele (henceforth referred to as Chd7+/− mice) phenocopy several aspects of CHARGE syndrome (Randall et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: Fgf8 expression in the IsO appeared reduced in Chd7+/− embryos
source: Fgf8 expression in the IsO appeared reduced in Chd7+/− embryos and was substantially downregulated in Chd7−/− embryos (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A-C

claim: Fgf8 expression was substantially downregulated in Chd7−/− embryos
source: Fgf8 expression in the IsO appeared reduced in Chd7+/− embryos and was substantially downregulated in Chd7−/− embryos (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A-C

claim: Fgf8 transcripts were reduced by 20% in Chd7+/− embryos
source: Quantitative RT-PCR analysis confirmed that Fgf8 transcripts were reduced by 20% in Chd7+/− embryos, and by 40% in Chd7−/− embryos (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Fgf8 transcripts were reduced by 40% in Chd7−/− embryos
source: Quantitative RT-PCR analysis confirmed that Fgf8 transcripts were reduced by 20% in Chd7+/− embryos, and by 40% in Chd7−/− embryos (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Fgf8 expression was reduced by 80% in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− embryos
source: Furthermore, Fgf8 expression was reduced by 80% in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− embryos, compared to 40% reduction in Chd7+/+;Fgf8+/− embryos (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Fgf8 expression was reduced by 40% in Chd7+/+;Fgf8+/− embryos
source: Furthermore, Fgf8 expression was reduced by 80% in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− embryos, compared to 40% reduction in Chd7+/+;Fgf8+/− embryos (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Etv5 is an FGF target gene
source: To ask whether this synergistic genetic interaction between Chd7 and Fgf8 loss-of-function alleles translated to defects in FGF signalling, the expression of the FGF target gene Etv5 was analysed (Roehl and Nusslein-Volhard, 2001; Yu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations

claim: Etv5 expression was clearly diminished in Chd7−/− embryos compared to wildtype controls
source: Whereas Etv5 expression was clearly diminished in Chd7−/− embryos compared to wildtype controls (Figure 1E,G), it did not appear substantially reduced in Chd7+/− embryos (Figure 1F), an observation confirmed by quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E-H

claim: Etv5 expression did not appear substantially reduced in Chd7+/− embryos
source: Whereas Etv5 expression was clearly diminished in Chd7−/− embryos compared to wildtype controls (Figure 1E,G), it did not appear substantially reduced in Chd7+/− embryos (Figure 1F), an observation confirmed by quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1F,H

claim: Etv5 expression was reduced by 50% in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− embryos
source: However, quantitative analyses showed that Etv5 expression was reduced by 50% in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− embryos, compared to wildtype levels in Chd7+/− and Fgf8+/− embryos (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H

claim: Etv5 expression was at wildtype levels in Chd7+/− embryos
source: However, quantitative analyses showed that Etv5 expression was reduced by 50% in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− embryos, compared to wildtype levels in Chd7+/− and Fgf8+/− embryos (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H

claim: Etv5 expression was at wildtype levels in Fgf8+/− embryos
source: However, quantitative analyses showed that Etv5 expression was reduced by 50% in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− embryos, compared to wildtype levels in Chd7+/− and Fgf8+/− embryos (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H

claim: CHD7 is an upstream regulator of Fgf8 in the IsO
source: These data identified CHD7 as an upstream regulator of Fgf8 in the IsO and revealed a synergistic relationship between the Chd7 and Fgf8 genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced Fgf8 expression in Chd7 mutants

claim: There is a synergistic relationship between the Chd7 and Fgf8 genes
source: These data identified CHD7 as an upstream regulator of Fgf8 in the IsO and revealed a synergistic relationship between the Chd7 and Fgf8 genes.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic interaction data showing enhanced phenotypes in double mutants

claim: The medial cerebellum (cerebellar vermis) is most sensitive to perturbations in FGF signalling during development
source: Previous studies have shown that the medial cerebellum, the cerebellar vermis, is most sensitive to perturbations in FGF signalling during development (Broccoli et al., 1999; Xu et al., 2000; Trokovic et al., 2003; Basson et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2011), hence we predicted that Chd7 deficiency will predispose embryos to cerebellar vermis defects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Cerebellar size was normal in Chd7+/− animals compared to wildtype littermates
source: Cerebellar size was normal in Chd7+/− and Fgf8+/− animals compared to wildtype littermates (Figure 2A–C), consistent with the observation that FGF signalling was not substantially reduced in these mutants (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: Cerebellar size was normal in Fgf8+/− animals compared to wildtype littermates
source: Cerebellar size was normal in Chd7+/− and Fgf8+/− animals compared to wildtype littermates (Figure 2A–C), consistent with the observation that FGF signalling was not substantially reduced in these mutants (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: Cerebellar foliation in the vermis and hemispheres appeared normal in Chd7+/− mutants
source: Furthermore, cerebellar foliation in the vermis and hemispheres appeared normal in the mutants (Figure 2A'–C',A"–C").
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2

claim: Cerebellar foliation in the vermis and hemispheres appeared normal in Fgf8+/− mutants
source: Furthermore, cerebellar foliation in the vermis and hemispheres appeared normal in the mutants (Figure 2A'–C',A"–C").
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2

claim: Chd7−/− embryos die by E11.5
source: As Chd7−/− embryos die by E11.5, cerebellar development could not be analysed in these mutants.
evidence: This is an observation from the study

claim: Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− animals survive
source: However, Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− animals survive and an analysis of cerebellar size revealed a significant reduction in size owing to vermis aplasia (Figure 2D,D',E).
evidence: This is an observation from the study

claim: Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− animals show a significant reduction in cerebellar size owing to vermis aplasia
source: However, Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− animals survive and an analysis of cerebellar size revealed a significant reduction in size owing to vermis aplasia (Figure 2D,D',E).
evidence: This is supported by volumetric analysis data shown in Figure 2D,D',E

claim: The cerebellar hemispheres were of normal size in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− animals
source: The cerebellar hemispheres were of normal size (Figure 2E) and had normal foliation compared to the controls (Figure 2D").
evidence: This is supported by volumetric and histological data shown in Figure 2E and 2D"

claim: The cerebellar hemispheres had normal foliation in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− animals
source: The cerebellar hemispheres were of normal size (Figure 2E) and had normal foliation compared to the controls (Figure 2D").
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2D"

claim: Cerebellar vermis aplasia in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− animals was already present at birth
source: Cerebellar vermis aplasia in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− animals was already present at birth, confirming that defects arose during embryonic development (Figure 2F–I,F'–I', red asterisk).
evidence: This is supported by data from P0 brains shown in Figure 2F-I

claim: The posterior midbrain (inferior colliculus) was abnormal in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− mutants
source: We also noted that the posterior midbrain (inferior colliculus), another region that is particularly sensitive to FGF signalling levels, was abnormal in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− mutants (Figure 2I', black asterisk).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2I'

claim: The inferior colliculus is a region that is particularly sensitive to FGF signalling levels
source: We also noted that the posterior midbrain (inferior colliculus), another region that is particularly sensitive to FGF signalling levels, was abnormal in Chd7+/−;Fgf8+/− mutants (Figure 2I', black asterisk).
evidence: This is established knowledge

claim: CHD7 is a SNF2H-like chromatin remodelling factor characterised by the presence of tandem chromodomains in its N-terminal region
source: The Chd7 gene encodes a SNF2H-like chromatin remodelling factor that is characterised by the presence of tandem chromodomains in its N-terminal region.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CHD7 protein structure

claim: CHD7 is recruited to distal gene regulatory elements
source: Genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation studies in cell lines have shown that CHD7 is recruited to distal gene regulatory elements, presumably through interactions between CHD7 chromodomains and methylated lysine 4 residues in histone 3 (H3K4me), present at regulatory elements (Schnetz et al., 2009, 2010; Engelen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous ChIP studies

claim: CHD7 is recruited to regulatory elements through interactions between CHD7 chromodomains and methylated lysine 4 residues in histone 3 (H3K4me)
source: Genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation studies in cell lines have shown that CHD7 is recruited to distal gene regulatory elements, presumably through interactions between CHD7 chromodomains and methylated lysine 4 residues in histone 3 (H3K4me), present at regulatory elements (Schnetz et al., 2009, 2010; Engelen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations and uses the word 'presumably' indicating some speculation

claim: The Drosophila homologue of the CHD7 subfamily is kismet
source: The Drosophila homologue of the CHD7 subfamily, kismet, was identified as a Trithorax gene and kismet mutants have reduced expression of homeotic genes and consequent transformations of body segments to more anterior structures (Daubresse et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation

claim: Kismet was identified as a Trithorax gene
source: The Drosophila homologue of the CHD7 subfamily, kismet, was identified as a Trithorax gene and kismet mutants have reduced expression of homeotic genes and consequent transformations of body segments to more anterior structures (Daubresse et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Daubresse et al., 1999

claim: Kismet mutants have reduced expression of homeotic genes
source: The Drosophila homologue of the CHD7 subfamily, kismet, was identified as a Trithorax gene and kismet mutants have reduced expression of homeotic genes and consequent transformations of body segments to more anterior structures (Daubresse et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Daubresse et al., 1999

claim: Kismet mutants have transformations of body segments to more anterior structures
source: The Drosophila homologue of the CHD7 subfamily, kismet, was identified as a Trithorax gene and kismet mutants have reduced expression of homeotic genes and consequent transformations of body segments to more anterior structures (Daubresse et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Daubresse et al., 1999

claim: Otx2 and Gbx2 influence anterior and posterior identity in the developing embryo, respectively
source: The homeobox genes Otx2 and Gbx2 influence anterior and posterior identity in the developing embryo, respectively, position the IsO and regulate the levels of Fgf8 expression (Broccoli et al., 1999; Hidalgo-Sanchez et al., 1999; Millet et al., 1999; Joyner et al., 2000; Heimbucher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Otx2 and Gbx2 position the IsO
source: The homeobox genes Otx2 and Gbx2 influence anterior and posterior identity in the developing embryo, respectively, position the IsO and regulate the levels of Fgf8 expression (Broccoli et al., 1999; Hidalgo-Sanchez et al., 1999; Millet et al., 1999; Joyner et al., 2000; Heimbucher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Otx2 and Gbx2 regulate the levels of Fgf8 expression
source: The homeobox genes Otx2 and Gbx2 influence anterior and posterior identity in the developing embryo, respectively, position the IsO and regulate the levels of Fgf8 expression (Broccoli et al., 1999; Hidalgo-Sanchez et al., 1999; Millet et al., 1999; Joyner et al., 2000; Heimbucher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Analysis of Chd7−/− mouse embryos at E8.25 (4ss) revealed Otx2 upregulation and posterior expansion of its expression
source: The analysis of Chd7−/− mouse embryos at E8.25 (4ss), shortly after the initiation of Fgf8 expression in the mes/r1 region revealed Otx2 upregulation and posterior expansion of its expression (Figure 3A,B, arrow indicating expanded expression).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: Krox20 expression is reduced in Chd7 mutant embryos
source: Although Krox20 expression is reduced in Chd7 mutant embryos (Alavizadeh et al., 2001), r3 was still clearly marked, confirming the expansion of Otx2 expression towards r3 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alavizadeh et al., 2001

claim: The expansion of Otx2 expression towards r3 was confirmed in Chd7−/− embryos
source: Although Krox20 expression is reduced in Chd7 mutant embryos (Alavizadeh et al., 2001), r3 was still clearly marked, confirming the expansion of Otx2 expression towards r3 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by combined in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3C,D

claim: The expansion of Otx2 expression included most of r1 in Chd7−/− embryos
source: Combined Otx2/Hoxa2 in situ hybridisation experiments suggested that the expansion of Otx2 expression included most of r1, as indicated by the absence of the Otx2/Hoxa2-negative r1 in Chd7−/− embryos (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by combined in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3E,F

claim: The Otx2/Hoxa2-negative r1 was absent in Chd7−/− embryos
source: Combined Otx2/Hoxa2 in situ hybridisation experiments suggested that the expansion of Otx2 expression included most of r1, as indicated by the absence of the Otx2/Hoxa2-negative r1 in Chd7−/− embryos (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by combined in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3E,F

claim: The posterior expansion of Otx2 expression in early Chd7−/− embryos was associated with reduced Fgf8 expression
source: We further confirmed that the posterior expansion of Otx2 expression in these early Chd7−/− embryos was associated with reduced Fgf8 expression (Figure 3G,H), in agreement with previously reported repression of Fgf8 expression by OTX2 (Acampora et al., 2001; Heimbucher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3G,H

claim: OTX2 represses Fgf8 expression
source: We further confirmed that the posterior expansion of Otx2 expression in these early Chd7−/− embryos was associated with reduced Fgf8 expression (Figure 3G,H), in agreement with previously reported repression of Fgf8 expression by OTX2 (Acampora et al., 2001; Heimbucher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Acampora et al., 2001; Heimbucher et al., 2007

claim: Fgf8 expression was initiated at the correct position in Chd7−/− embryos
source: A side-by-side comparison of stage-matched embryos indicated that Fgf8 expression was initiated at the correct position in Chd7−/− embryos (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3I,J

claim: The posterior expansion of Otx2 expression was not associated with a re-positioning of the IsO in Chd7−/− embryos
source: This observation showed that the posterior expansion of Otx2 expression was not associated with a re-positioning of the IsO and indicated that Otx2 was mis-expressed in the anterior hindbrain of Chd7−/− embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Fgf8 expression was initiated at the correct position

claim: Otx2 was mis-expressed in the anterior hindbrain of Chd7−/− embryos
source: This observation showed that the posterior expansion of Otx2 expression was not associated with a re-positioning of the IsO and indicated that Otx2 was mis-expressed in the anterior hindbrain of Chd7−/− embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Otx2 expanded posteriorly without repositioning the IsO

claim: Gbx2 is a marker of r1
